China's jewellery counter is not tracking the gold price under it — it is pulling away from it.

The Shanghai Gold Exchange closed Au99.99 at 940.72 yuan a gram on 14 August, down 0.90% on the day. Chow Tai Fook's counter read 1,312 yuan the same day, down 2.09% — more than twice the exchange's fall, but from a much higher base. This paper published the same pair on 9 August at 938 and 1,286, a 37.10% markup. Six days later the exchange has moved 0.29% and the counter has moved 2.02%. The gap did not close; it widened by 23.28 yuan a gram, to a 39.47% markup.

On the readings this desk can verify, the Chinese jewellery markup has run between 37.10% and 41.17% this month — and it is currently near the top of that range while the metal itself is falling. China's gold jewellery consumption fell to its lowest since 2004, reported here on 3 August. A counter charging more while its customers buy less is a merchant setting a margin, not a market clearing.

This paper has now refused Kitco's platinum mark twice — and today it took it anyway, on the record.

On 12 August the cell was stale. On 13 August it was live but sat $14.60 below TradingEconomics and JM Bullion, which agreed with each other to within 50 cents. At 04:59 this morning the tape desk found the same shape a third time and made the call: platinum is written back on Kitco at $1,725.00, palladium with it at $1,297.00, gold at $4,356.20 and silver at $64.77 — all four marks, one board, struck at 06:00 New York time.

At the bench that works out to $140.05 a gram of fine gold, $2.08 a gram of fine silver, $55.46 a gram of fine platinum and $41.70 a gram of fine palladium. Palladium's move today, 1.67% down, is the tape's largest single-day swing — and it comes off a mark that had itself been held for two sessions. A rule that stops this paper printing a number it cannot stand behind is not the same as a rule that stops it printing numbers.

The marginal buyer of gold in July was European — and a paper that prints a dollar-an-ounce number every morning without naming that buyer is reporting half the market.

Global gold ETFs took in $3 billion in July, reversing two months of outflow. The regional split is the finding: Europe took $2 billion, with the UK alone at $875 million and Switzerland at $657 million. Asia took $616 million, China the strongest contributor, Japan in outflow. North America — the world's largest fund market — took just $71 million for the entire month.

Set against the physical side, the year stops looking contradictory. Global jewellery demand fell to 278 tonnes in Q2, the smallest since the pandemic, reported here 31 July. India's gold jewellery demand fell 15% by weight the same day; China's fell to its lowest since 2004, reported 3 August. The jewellery counter is shrinking in India and China, the bar buyer is heavy in China, and the fund buyer, this month, was British and Swiss. Holdings remain 108 tonnes below February's record — one month of inflow hasn't undone the year's withdrawal.
